summary: The note recounts how the municipality of Maplewood went from ecological indifference to leadership in wildlife protection and habitat restoration between September 2023 and April 2024. It covers nature walks, river restoration, urban micro-habitats, a wildlife corridor, the return of meadowlarks, and new school curricula, driven by figures like Sarah Jennings, Dr. Raymond Brooks and Emma Rodriguez. It closes with smaller initiatives and newer projects such as the Butterfly Byway and the Urban Fruit Forest.
one_line: Maplewood's residents and groups, led by Jennings, Brooks and Rodriguez, built wildlife and habitat projects that brought back locally extinct meadowlarks.
key_facts: Sarah Jennings, a local teacher and naturalist, organized the first "Walk with Wildlife" event in late September 2023 and led the Wildlife Watchers group.
The Wildlife Watchers' walks took attendees through endangered scrublands next to the Elkwood River; by early October hundreds of residents attended regularly.
Retired ecologist Dr. Raymond Brooks and citizen scientists launched "Operation Green Veins" on November 15, 2023, to rehabilitate waterways by reintroducing native plants along the Elkwood River.
Operation Green Veins stabilized the riverbanks and provided habitat, with dragonflies seen among newly planted bulrushes and cattails.
The Haven Project was unveiled on December 6, 2023, spearheaded by wildlife conservationist Emma Rodriguez, creating micro-habitats on abandoned lots and neglected public spaces.
Residents and local businesses donated space, resources and time to The Haven Project, whose sites include educational signs and interactive workshops.
The Maplewood Wildlife Corridor began on January 1, 2024, as the idea of the environmental activist group "Green Alliance".

The corridor stretches from northern forested reserves to southern wetlands using private land easements, public park linkages and habitat patches, with the Green Alliance coordinating with city planners.
Meadowlarks, declared locally extinct nearly a decade earlier, returned in April 2024 thanks to grassland restoration and pesticide-free zones.
Bird watchers from across the state came to see the meadowlarks' return.
After the meadowlarks returned, the city's education system added a local ecology curriculum led by Jennings, with schoolgrounds turned into native plant gardens and rooftops hosting apiaries.
Newer projects include the Butterfly Byway and the Urban Fruit Forest, and Brooks, Rodriguez and Jennings inspired neighboring communities.
